analysis|03-05|1946|Ο Τσόρτσιλ μιλά για το «σιδηρούν παραπέτασμα»|Churchill speaks of the "Iron Curtain"|At the end of the Second World War the Soviet Union had extended its influence over Eastern Europe, while its relations with the Western powers were deteriorating quickly. Europe had been divided into spheres of influence, and the Western countries were strengthening their alliances. // On 5 March 1946, at Fulton in Missouri in the United States, Winston Churchill spoke at a university and described an "Iron Curtain" that divided continental Europe. The speech addressed both public opinion and the political leadership, and it provoked strong reactions in Moscow. // The expression became a symbol of the Cold War and influenced the strategy of the United States and its allies, until the founding of NATO in 1949. The term remains common in the history of the period and shows how the division of Europe was imprinted on the language of diplomacy.

analysis|03-05|1953|Πεθαίνει ο Στάλιν|Stalin dies|Joseph Stalin ruled the Soviet Union for almost three decades, with violent purges, the concentration of power and rapid industrialisation at an enormous human cost. His leadership combined rapid development with the suppression of every dissenting voice within the party. In his last years the repression continued, with new trials and persecutions. // On 5 March 1953 Stalin died in Moscow after a stroke, and for several hours he received no immediate medical help. His death occurred at a time of political uncertainty about the future of the regime. The announcement was made through an official bulletin, and power was briefly shared among leaders of the party leadership. // His death opened the period of de-Stalinisation, with an easing of repression and public debate about the crimes of the past. In the years that followed power remained concentrated, and the post-Stalin era changed the relationship between the state and the population without a complete change of the system.

analysis|03-06|1521|Ο Μαγγελάνος φτάνει στο Γκουάμ|Magellan reaches Guam|Ferdinand Magellan, a Portuguese navigator in the service of Spain, set out in 1519 on a voyage aimed at reaching the spice islands from the west. Spain, which had financed the expedition, wanted a route to the spices that did not pass through Portuguese territory. Magellan had previously served the Portuguese empire, but had left after disagreements. // On 6 March 1521 the expedition reached the island of Guam, where contact with the locals was brief and often tense. The Europeans obtained food and then continued the voyage, without staying for a long period. The expedition had initially five ships, but their number was greatly reduced during the voyage. // Guam became one of the first points of contact between Europe and the islands of the Pacific. Magellan was killed shortly afterwards in the Philippines, but the voyage was completed by his companions, who became the first to circumnavigate the Earth. The voyage proved that the ocean could be crossed with ships of the era, at great cost.

analysis|03-06|1820|Ο Συμβιβασμός του Μιζούρι|The Missouri Compromise|In the early nineteenth century the balance between the slave-holding and the free states of the United States was delicate, and the rivalry reflected different economies. Missouri asked to enter the Union as a slave state, and Congress debated how to handle the extension of slavery into the new territories. // The agreement adopted in 1820 admitted Missouri as a slave state and at the same time Maine as a free state, keeping the balance in the Senate. A latitude line was set, north of which slavery was prohibited in the remaining territories of Louisiana. President Monroe signed the law, and many regarded it as a temporary solution. // The compromise secured relative calm for about three decades, but it did not resolve the question of slavery. Its collapse opened the way to new conflicts and to the rise of the political movement that opposed slavery. It was overturned by the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854, and the crisis that followed eventually led to the Civil War.

analysis|03-06|1836|Πέφτει το Αλαμό|The fall of the Alamo|After the declaration of Texan independence, the Alamo fort in San Antonio had become the centre of the settlers' resistance. A small garrison of volunteers defended the fort, which had strategic importance. The military weakness of the revolution was evident, with small armies and limited supplies. // On 6 March 1836 the Mexican army, led by Antonio López de Santa Anna, attacked the fort after a siege that had lasted several days. The defenders knew that reinforcements were uncertain, but they remained at their posts. David Crockett and James Bowie were killed, and the battle became a symbol of Texan sacrifice. // The fall of the Alamo intensified the anger of the Texans and became the occasion for the slogan "Remember the Alamo". A few weeks later, at San Jacinto, the Texans defeated the Mexican army, and Texas gained its independence. The memory of the Alamo was used to strengthen the national identity of Texas.

analysis|03-06|1857|Η απόφαση Ντρεντ Σκοτ|The Dred Scott decision|Dred Scott was an enslaved man who had lived with his owner in states and territories where slavery was prohibited, and he asked a court for his freedom and that of his family. The case was among the most charged legal issues of the era, since Congress had enacted different rules for the territories. // On 6 March 1857 the Supreme Court of the United States decided by a majority that African Americans could not be citizens of the United States and that Congress had no power to prohibit slavery in the territories. The minority argued that slavery was not a matter that the court should resolve. // The decision provoked fierce reaction in the North and intensified the divisive atmosphere before the Civil War, effectively annulling the Missouri Compromise. Later, the constitutional amendments after the war nullified its consequences, recognising citizenship for all who were born or naturalised in the United States.

analysis|03-06|1899|Πατεντάρεται η ασπιρίνη|Aspirin is patented|At the end of the nineteenth century the German chemical industry was growing rapidly, and companies were seeking new drugs based on synthetic substances. Salicylic acid was known for relieving pain and fever, but it caused stomach irritation, which limited its use. // In the laboratory of the Bayer company the chemist Felix Hoffmann had synthesised a gentler form of the substance, acetylsalicylic acid, which the company registered under the trade name Aspirin. On 6 March 1899 the registration of the name became official. The new compound was gentler on the stomach, which opened the way to wide use. // The drug became one of the most widely used in the world, for pain and fever and later for the prevention of thromboses. The case shows how a synthetic substance can change medical practice and everyday life, although its use requires medical supervision.

analysis|03-06|1957|Ανεξαρτησία της Γκάνας|Ghana becomes independent|After the Second World War the colonial powers of Africa faced strong pressure for independence. The Gold Coast was of great economic importance because of its cocoa production, and the party of Kwame Nkrumah won the elections and demanded self-government. // On 6 March 1957 the colony became independent under the name Ghana, with Nkrumah heading the government. The ceremony was attended by leaders from other countries, and the flag of the new country was raised in the capital. The proclamation was a milestone, since Ghana was the first state of sub-Saharan Africa to gain independence from European colonial rule. // Ghana's independence influenced the liberation movements in many African countries and strengthened the idea of African unity. Nkrumah became a symbol of Pan-Africanism, although the country's later course went through political crises and military coups.

analysis|03-07|1876|Το δίπλωμα του τηλεφώνου|The telephone patent|In the mid-nineteenth century telegraphy was the main means of communication over long distances, but it required trained operators. Alexander Graham Bell, a teacher of speech for the deaf, was investigating ways of transmitting sound by electric current, and the era was full of competing inventions. // On 7 March 1876 Bell received a United States patent for the device that transmitted human speech through a wire. The process was complex and was accompanied by disputes, since other researchers had similar ideas. // The invention laid the foundations of modern telephony, which transformed communication and the economy. The networks that were created affected the organisation of business and everyday life, and the telephone soon became a daily tool all over the world.

analysis|03-07|1936|Η Γερμανία μπαίνει στη Ρηνανία|Germany enters the Rhineland|After the First World War the Treaty of Versailles had demilitarised the Rhineland, the area west of the Rhine in Germany. The prohibition on a military presence was regarded as a security guarantee for France, and Hitler, who had taken power in 1933, was challenging the terms of the treaty. // On 7 March 1936 German troops entered the demilitarised zone, in an act that violated the treaty and the Locarno agreement. France sent protests but did not react militarily, while Britain hesitated to act. The German government presented the move as a defensive measure. // The absence of a reaction is regarded as a turning point, since it encouraged Hitler to proceed with new expansionist moves. The success of the move strengthened Hitler's position at home, and the events contributed to the escalation that finally led to the Second World War.

analysis|03-07|1965|Η «Ματωμένη Κυριακή» στο Σέλμα|"Bloody Sunday" in Selma|In Selma, Alabama, African Americans faced legal and practical restrictions on voting, despite constitutional guarantees. Alabama had a long history of institutional segregation, and black participation in elections was very low. // On 7 March 1965 a peaceful march towards Montgomery crossed the Edmund Pettus Bridge and was met by state troopers with tear gas and beatings. Many marchers were injured, and the images were broadcast on television across the nation. // "Bloody Sunday" moved public opinion and led to new marches, with the participation of Martin Luther King Jr. A few months later Congress passed the Voting Rights Act, which removed many of the obstacles to African American voting.

analysis|03-08|1917|Η Επανάσταση του Φεβρουαρίου|The February Revolution|In 1917 Russia had been at war for three years, with huge losses, food shortages and deep discontent. The government had failed to carry out reforms, and Tsar Nicholas II had personally taken command of the army. // In early March, according to the new calendar, demonstrations by women and workers broke out in Petrograd and developed into a general uprising within a few days. Military units refused to fire on the demonstrators, and the capital passed under the control of the revolutionaries. // The revolution led to the abdication of Nicholas II on 15 March and to the end of the Romanov monarchy. The Provisional Committee of the Duma took power, while the soviets also operated, and this dual power set the tone for the following period.

analysis|03-08|1957|Ξανανοίγει η Διώρυγα του Σουέζ|The Suez Canal reopens|The Suez Canal opened in 1869 and became a vital route for trade between Europe and Asia. Egypt regarded the canal as critical for its national independence, while the Western powers had historically controlled the shares. // In 1956 Egypt nationalised the company that managed it, and Britain, France and Israel intervened militarily. During the crisis the canal had been blocked by sunken ships, and clearing work began immediately afterwards. // The intervention provoked international pressure, and the forces withdrew. The reopening of the canal in March 1957 restored the flow of trade, although the crisis changed the political balance in the Middle East. Egypt was strengthened as a regional leader, while Britain and France lost part of their influence.

analysis|03-08|1965|Οι πρώτοι αμερικανικοί στρατιώτες στο Βιετνάμ|The first American soldiers in Vietnam|Until 1965 American involvement in the Vietnam War was limited to advisers and to equipment supporting the army of South Vietnam. The American government believed that communist expansion in Asia had to be halted, in line with the domino theory. // On 8 March 1965 about 3,500 marines landed near Da Nang, forming the first American combat troops on the Asian mainland. The initial mission had a protective character for the air bases, but it quickly developed into extensive involvement. // The decision opened the period of massive American involvement, which reached hundreds of thousands of soldiers in the years that followed. The war caused enormous human and material losses and strengthened the anti-war movement in the United States and in other countries.

analysis|03-08|2014|Εξαφανίζεται η πτήση MH370|Flight MH370 disappears|Flight MH370 of Malaysia Airlines was a Boeing 777 on a route from Kuala Lumpur to Beijing. The take-off took place normally, and the aircraft had not signalled any problem before it lost contact with air traffic control. // On 8 March 2014 the aircraft disappeared over the sea, with 239 people on board. The searches focused on a large area of the Indian Ocean, and the search was among the most expensive in the history of aviation, without the whole aircraft being found. // The only confirmed findings were fragments washed up on the shores of the Indian Ocean. The disappearance remains a mystery and has given rise to many theories, while the families of the passengers continue to demand answers.

analysis|03-09|1230|Η μάχη της Κλοκοτνίτσας|The battle of Klokotnitsa|After the Fourth Crusade and the collapse of Constantinople, several states emerged in the Balkans, among them the Despotate of Epirus and Bulgaria. Theodore Komnenos Doukas of Epirus was expanding to the north and east, threatening Bulgarian territories. // On 9 March 1230 Ivan Asen II of Bulgaria defeated Theodore at the battle of Klokotnitsa. Theodore was captured, and Epirus lost a significant part of its conquests in Thrace and Macedonia. The two rulers had invoked different rights of influence in the Balkans. // The victory strengthened Bulgaria, which for a time became the strongest power in the region. Epirus recovered later, and the balance of the Balkans remained fluid for decades. The battle occupies a central place in the history of the states that emerged after the Fall of 1204.

analysis|03-09|1776|Εκδίδεται ο «Πλούτος των Εθνών»|"The Wealth of Nations" is published|In the eighteenth century economic thought was still linked with mercantilism and with state control of trade. Ideas about the free market began to spread in Britain, and the Scottish philosopher Adam Smith studied the economies of nations. Smith had taught moral philosophy at the University of Glasgow. // On 9 March 1776 his work "An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations" was published. Smith argued that prosperity comes from labour, from the division of labour and from free exchange, and that the market operates through an "invisible hand". The work is divided into five books. // The book is regarded as the foundation of classical economic thought and influenced liberal political economy for centuries. It has been the subject of debate about the role of the state, and many modern economists regard it as the starting point of the discipline.

analysis|03-09|1796|Ο Ναπολέων παντρεύεται την Ιωσηφίνα|Napoleon marries Josephine|At the end of 1795 the young Napoleon Bonaparte had gained fame after his decisive intervention in Paris, and the French Revolution had passed into the phase of the Directory. Joséphine de Beauharnais was the widow of Alexandre de Beauharnais, who had been executed during the Terror. // On 9 March 1796 Napoleon and Joséphine married in Paris, in a civil ceremony. The command for the Italian campaign was given to the young general shortly before his wedding, and a few days later he left for Italy. // The marriage linked the young general with the social circles of the era and proved useful for his career. Joséphine later played a role in shaping Napoleon's image. Their relationship was turbulent, and the couple separated in 1809, when Napoleon decided that he needed an heir.

analysis|03-09|1959|Εμφανίζεται η Μπάρμπι|Barbie makes her appearance|At the end of the 1950s the toy market in the United States was largely oriented towards baby dolls, and girls had a limited choice. Ruth Handler, co-founder of the Mattel company, wanted to create a doll in adult form, so that children would have a frame for their imagination. // On 9 March 1959 the Barbie doll was presented at the New York Toy Fair, with outfits and accessories that set off her form. Its launch was impressive and quickly attracted a wide audience. The doll took the name of Handler's daughter, Barbara. // Barbie became one of the best-known toys in the world, with many professions and versions, and became a subject of debate about physical image and gender stereotypes. Her history shows how a product can influence social perceptions for many decades.

analysis|03-09|1959|Παρουσιάζεται η κούκλα Barbie|The Barbie doll is presented|At the end of the 1950s the Mattel company was looking for new products for the children's market. Ruth Handler noticed that girls played with paper dolls of adults and wanted a similar doll made of plastic. Mattel had already made its toys known through television advertising. // The doll was presented on 9 March 1959 at the New York toy fair and took the name of Handler's daughter. Its release was accompanied by an advertising campaign, something new for the era. The positive reception showed that the idea had appeal. // In the decades that followed Barbie became a global brand, with constant changes in fashion and in professions. Over the years the company developed a whole universe of accessories and stories around the doll. The doll still receives criticism for her figure, while others regard her as a symbol of children's imagination.

analysis|03-10|1762|Εκτελείται ο Ζαν Καλάς|Jean Calas is executed|In eighteenth-century Toulouse the Protestant merchant Jean Calas lived in a Catholic environment, with intense religious tensions. His family were cloth merchants, and their relationship with the local community was sensitive. // When his son was found dead in 1761, the justice system claimed that the young man had been killed by his father, because he wanted to prevent his conversion to Catholicism. Calas was sentenced to a brutal death and was executed in March 1762. The trial had relied on testimonies that were later disputed. // The case provoked a great reaction in Europe, and Voltaire launched a campaign to restore his name. Calas's acquittal in 1765 became a symbol of tolerance, and the case was linked with criticism of the judicial system of the era.

analysis|03-10|1876|Η πρώτη τηλεφωνική κλήση|The first telephone call|Graham Bell worked in his laboratory in Boston on a device that transmitted sound through an electric circuit, financed by business circles. His assistant was the electrician Thomas Watson, who handled the circuits and the devices. // On 10 March 1876, while experimenting with the device, Bell accidentally spilled acid on his clothes and called his assistant in another room, saying the phrase "Mr Watson, come here, I want you". Watson heard him through the device and the communication succeeded. // The first telephone call was the initial step in the history of telephony, and Bell later developed the network and the company. The simple everyday phrase gave the event a symbolic character, and the telephone became a basic tool of society.

analysis|03-10|1945|Ο βομβαρδισμός του Τόκιο|The bombing of Tokyo|In the final stages of the war in the Pacific, American aircraft used low-altitude bombers to start fires in densely populated cities. The strategy aimed at destroying industry and infrastructure, but the cost for the civilian population was enormous. // In Tokyo, during the night of 9 to 10 March 1945, incendiary bombs caused a huge fire that spread through the city's districts, and the Shitamachi area was among the most affected. More than one hundred thousand people, mainly civilians, were killed, and thousands were left homeless. // The attack is regarded as one of the deadliest single attacks of the war and is used today in discussions about the legality of bombing and the protection of civilians. The memory of the destruction remains alive in Japan, in museums and in the testimonies of survivors.

analysis|03-10|2019|Συντρίβεται αεροπλάνο της Ethiopian Airlines|The Ethiopian Airlines aircraft crashes|The Boeing 737 MAX was the newest version of the 737 family, with larger engines that changed the aircraft's aerodynamics. After its introduction, an automatic system called MCAS had become the subject of questions about the control of the aircraft. Ethiopian Airlines was one of the largest airlines in Africa and had ordered several aircraft of the type. // On 10 March 2019 flight ET302 took off from Addis Ababa and a few minutes later lost height and crashed near the town of Bishoftu. All 157 people on board were killed, among them citizens of dozens of countries. The similarity with the Lion Air crash in Indonesia a few months earlier heightened the concerns. // Many countries temporarily banned flights of the type, and Boeing revised the system's software and the training of pilots. The investigations reached findings about the design and certification of the aircraft. The incident changed the cooperation of regulatory authorities around the world.

analysis|03-11|1851|Η πρεμιέρα του Ριγκολέτο|The premiere of Rigoletto|In the mid-nineteenth century Italian opera was the most popular musical genre in Europe, and Giuseppe Verdi had already gained fame with dramatic works. The authorities often imposed censorship on librettos, because they feared references to power. // Rigoletto was based on Victor Hugo's drama "The King Amuses Himself" and tells the story of a court jester who loses his daughter. The premiere took place in Venice, at the La Fenice theatre, on 11 March 1851, and changes to the libretto were requested. // The work is regarded today as one of the most important of the Italian repertoire, with well-known arias such as "La donna è mobile". Its success strengthened Verdi's position in international opera.

analysis|03-11|1867|Πρώτη παράσταση του «Δον Κάρλος» στο Παρίσι|The first performance of Don Carlos in Paris|At the end of the 1860s Paris was the centre of international opera, with the Grand Opéra attracting composers from all over Europe. Verdi wrote a work for the French stage, with dances, large ensembles and extensive sets. // Don Carlos is based on a play by Schiller about the Spanish prince and his conflict with his father, against a background of political and religious violence. The premiere on 11 March 1867 was very long and had a lavish production, and the audience reacted positively. // The work remains one of the most discussed of Verdi's, because there are different versions, in Italian and in French. Its form influenced the great productions of the era in Europe.

analysis|03-11|1983|Το Πακιστάν δοκιμάζει πυρηνικό όπλο|Pakistan tests a nuclear weapon|In the early 1980s Pakistan was in tension with India, which had carried out a nuclear test in 1974. Islamabad wanted to acquire a similar deterrent capability, and its programme was advancing in secret. The regional balance was the central motive. // The test of 11 March 1983 was not officially announced at the time, and its details became known gradually and with delay. This secrecy heightened the concerns of the neighbours. // In 1998 Pakistan and India carried out tests within a short period, and the nuclear balance in South Asia became an international matter of concern. This development left deep marks on international security.

analysis|03-11|1985|Ο Γκορμπατσόφ γίνεται γενικός γραμματέας|Gorbachev becomes general secretary|In the 1980s the Soviet Union faced economic stagnation and industrial shortages. Brezhnev's successors died within a short period, and the leadership was elderly. This situation created a need for renewal. // On 11 March 1985 the leadership of the Communist Party elected Mikhail Gorbachev general secretary. The new leader, younger than his predecessors, introduced perestroika for the economy and glasnost for transparency. // The reforms led to the weakening of party control, to the rise of national movements and to the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991. The fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989 deeply affected Europe.

analysis|03-11|2011|Σεισμός και τσουνάμι στην Ιαπωνία|Earthquake and tsunami in Japan|Japan lies in an area of intense seismic activity, at the point where tectonic plates converge. Several nuclear power plants are located near the coast, using seawater for cooling. The geography of the country made the dangers particularly significant. // On 11 March 2011 an earthquake of magnitude 9 struck off the coast of Tohoku, and a tsunami followed that destroyed towns and villages. Thousands of people were killed or went missing. The Fukushima Daiichi plant lost its cooling, with partial melting of the fuel in three reactors and the release of radiation. // Thousands of people left their homes, and resettlement is still under way. Japan temporarily shut down all its reactors, and many countries revised their nuclear policies.

analysis|03-12|1918|Η Μόσχα ξαναγίνεται πρωτεύουσα της Ρωσίας|Moscow becomes the capital of Russia again|In March 1918 Russia was in turmoil after the October Revolution of 1917. Saint Petersburg, the capital since 1712, was close to the front, and the government feared the German advance. This threat made the change of capital imperative. // In early March 1918 the Bolsheviks decided to move the government to Moscow, a safer centre. The move took place within a few days, and Lenin settled in the Kremlin. // Moscow has remained the capital to this day. The choice symbolised the need for centralised control in an era of civil war and determined the centre of the Soviet state.

analysis|03-12|1930|Ξεκινά η Πορεία του Αλατιού|The Salt March begins|In 1930 the British colonial government of India held a monopoly on the production and sale of salt, with a tax that burdened the poor. Gandhi demanded the abolition of the tax as a symbol of colonial oppression. This demand combined the economic and the political dimension. // On 12 March 1930 Gandhi set out on a march from his ashram at Sabarmati towards the sea at Dandi. The march lasted almost three weeks, and in every village the residents welcomed the marchers. On 6 April Gandhi gathered salt from the sea, breaking the law. // The act provoked thousands of arrests and intense international attention. Salt became a symbol of national resistance, and the march later influenced movements of non-violent protest.

analysis|03-12|1938|Το Άνσλους|The Anschluss|After the First World War Austria had lost much of its empire, and many Austrians wished for union with Germany. The Treaty of Versailles had prohibited the union. // In March 1938 Hitler pressed Chancellor Schuschnigg to resign. On 12 March German troops entered Austria without serious resistance, and the union, known as the Anschluss, was officially announced. Arrests and persecutions of Jews and political opponents followed. // The annexation strengthened the position of Nazi Germany in Central Europe. The absence of a reaction from the Western powers was later the subject of criticism. After the war Austria was recognised as the "first victim" of Nazism, although the participation of many Austrians remained a subject of debate.

analysis|03-13|1781|Ο Γουίλιαμ Χέρσελ ανακαλύπτει τον πλανήτη Ουρανό|William Herschel discovers the planet Uranus|On 13 March 1781 William Herschel, a musician in Bath, England, who had turned to astronomy and built his own telescopes, observed an object that looked like a star but moved slowly among the stars. In the eighteenth century the known planets were those visible to the naked eye since antiquity. This observation changed the data. // After confirmations, astronomers concluded that it was a new planet, which was initially named Georgium Sidus and later Uranus. It was the first time that a new planet had been located with a telescope. // The discovery widened the understanding of the solar system. Herschel was appointed King's Astronomer, and this position gave him the resources for later research.

analysis|03-13|1881|Δολοφονείται ο τσάρος Αλέξανδρος Β΄|Tsar Alexander II is assassinated|In Russia of the 1870s the revolutionary organisation "People's Will" believed that the murder of the tsar would provoke an uprising. Alexander II had already emancipated the serfs, but repression continued. This contradiction made violence seem to the conspirators to be logical. // On 13 March 1881 members of the organisation threw a bomb at his carriage in Saint Petersburg. The tsar was mortally wounded shortly afterwards, when a second bomb exploded. // His death led to stricter measures against the opposition and to the strengthening of the police. His successor, Alexander III, followed a policy of counter-reforms.

analysis|03-13|1930|Ανακοινώνεται ο Πλούτωνας|Pluto is announced|Pluto was discovered in 1930 at the Lowell Observatory in Arizona, after many years of searching for a "Planet X" that would explain the disturbances in the orbits of Uranus and Neptune. Clyde Tombaugh analysed the photographic plates and located the object. The search was long and demanding. // The new celestial body was named by an Oxford schoolgirl, and the announcement was made on 13 March 1930. The name was linked with the mythological deity of the underworld. // Pluto's mass was much smaller than had been calculated, and in 2006 the International Astronomical Union classified it as a dwarf planet. That decision changed the classification of the solar system.

analysis|03-13|1957|Επίθεση φοιτητών στο προεδρικό μέγαρο της Αβάνας|Students attack the presidential palace in Havana|In 1957 Cuba was under the regime of Fulgencio Batista, with intense political repression and resistance from student groups. The revolutionaries believed that a violent action would provoke an uprising. The opposition was divided over the methods. // On 13 March 1957 a group of students attacked the presidential palace in Havana, while others tried to enter the radio station. Batista escaped, and the attack failed, with heavy losses. // The attack showed the determination of the opposition, which a few years later overthrew the regime in the revolution of 1959. The attempt of 1957 is regarded as one of the first steps in that process.

analysis|03-13|1992|Σεισμός στο Ερζιντζάν|Erzincan earthquake|North-eastern Turkey lies in a seismic zone, near the Anatolian fault, and many buildings in the area had not been designed for strong tremors. The town of Erzincan had suffered earlier earthquakes in its history. The vulnerability of the area was known. // The earthquake of 1992 struck the area with great force, killing hundreds of people and leaving a large number of residents homeless. Buildings of concrete and brick collapsed, and rescue teams had difficulty reaching the more remote villages. // The disaster showed the need for stricter anti-seismic rules and for better preparation by the authorities. The event contributed to the debate on reconstruction and on the protection of settlements in seismic areas of Turkey.

analysis|03-14|1794|Το δίπλωμα του Ίλαϊ Γουίτνεϊ|Eli Whitney's patent|Eli Whitney was an American inventor who had moved to the South, where cotton cultivation was steadily increasing. The manual separation of the seeds from the fibres was slow and expensive. This need gave the motivation for his invention. // On 14 March 1794 he received a patent for a machine that separated the fibres with wire teeth and brushes. The invention was simple but effective. // The machine increased cotton production, which strengthened the economy of the South and, indirectly, the importance of slavery. Whitney did not earn the expected profits from the patent.

analysis|03-14|1879|Γεννιέται ο Άλμπερτ Αϊνστάιν|Albert Einstein is born|Albert Einstein was born on 14 March 1879 in Ulm, Germany, into a family of merchants. At a young age he showed an interest in mathematics and physics, and his curiosity about the phenomena of nature remained steady throughout his life. His family background was typical for the era, with no signs that foreshadowed the distinction. // As a young clerk at the patent office in Bern, he formulated the special theory of relativity in 1905. This theory changed the understanding of space and time, and his work at the office allowed him to think in peace. // He later developed the general theory, which described gravity as the curvature of spacetime. This theory was confirmed by observations in the following decade and became the basis of modern cosmology. // In 1921 he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on the photoelectric effect, and not for the theories of relativity. His theory profoundly changed cosmology and modern physics, and his legacy continues to influence contemporary research.
